overview.text: Hikaru Genji, often translated as “Shining Genji,” is the fictional protagonist of Murasaki Shikibu’s early-eleventh-century Heian-period novel The Tale of Genji. In the story, he is born a son of Emperor Kiritsubo but gives up royal status and receives the surname Minamoto. Celebrated for his beauty, sensitivity, poetic talent, and romances, he represents an aristocratic ideal, while the narrative also explores complicated feelings and relationships. His life unfolds in the refined court society around Heian-kyō, today’s Kyoto; important relationships include those with his first wife, Aoi, and lifelong companion, Lady Murasaki. Genji is a literary creation, not a historical prince, and his central role makes him one of Japanese literature’s most memorable characters.

key_facts.text: “Hikaru Genji” means “Shining Genji”; the National Diet Library says his exceptional beauty earned him this name and the related title “Shining Prince.”
In the tale, Genji is the son of Emperor Kiritsubo, relinquishes royal status, and receives the surname Minamoto.
His poetic nature, gentleness, beauty, and romances make him an idealized figure in the story.
The tale’s settings include real places in and around Heian-kyō, the former capital now known as Kyoto.
Genji is fictional. The National Diet Library lists several possible historical inspirations, not one definitive real-life identity.
